concepts.def: A cell contains chemicals which react to produce electricity. The electricity is not stored inside the cell in advance; it is produced while the reaction between the chemicals is happening, and it lasts only for as long as that reaction can continue.

One of the two conducting pieces, usually metals, that dip into the electrolyte and connect the chemicals in the cell to the external circuit. The type of electrode used is one of the factors the voltage of the cell depends on.

The liquid or solution containing free-moving ions in which the electrodes are placed. It is not simply a means of joining the electrodes: the type of electrolyte is one of the factors that determines the voltage the cell produces.

The potential difference the cell produces, measured with a voltmeter connected across it. It is dependent upon a number of factors, including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte used. It does not depend on how large the pieces of electrode are.

A cell made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Both conditions matter: the two metals must be different from each other, and they must be in contact with an electrolyte rather than with air or with pure water.
Two or more cells connected together in series. Everyday speech calls a single cell a battery, but in chemistry a battery is the combination of cells, not one cell on its own.

Connecting cells one after another, positive terminal to negative terminal. Cells are connected in series in a battery to provide a greater voltage than a single cell can: the voltages of the individual cells add together.

A cell in which the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Once that reactant is gone the cell cannot produce electricity again, and supplying an external current will not restart it.

The everyday battery named by the specification as an example of the non-rechargeable type. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable: when a reactant inside has been used up the battery is finished and must be disposed of or recycled.

A cell that can be recharged because the chemical reactions inside it are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. The reactants are re-formed from the products, so the cell can produce electricity again.

Supplying an external electrical current to a rechargeable cell or battery. The current drives the chemical reactions backwards, turning the products of the discharge reaction back into the reactants. No new chemicals are added to the cell.

When cells are made from pairs of metals in the same electrolyte, the voltage produced depends on how far apart the two metals are in the reactivity series. The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage of the cell.

In a simple cell made from two different metals, the more reactive metal is the negative electrode: it is the metal that loses electrons more readily. Voltage data for pairs of metals can therefore be used to place the metals in order of reactivity.

Weighing up the advantages and disadvantages of a cell for a given job. A non-rechargeable cell is cheap and ready to use but is thrown away once a reactant is used up; a rechargeable cell costs more at first but is used many times, so it produces less waste.

A cell supplied by an external source of fuel, for example hydrogen, and oxygen or air. Because the fuel comes from outside, the cell keeps producing electricity for as long as the fuel and oxygen are supplied, rather than stopping when an internal reactant is used up.

Inside a fuel cell the fuel is oxidised electrochemically rather than burned. The oxidation takes place at an electrode, so the electrons transferred pass through the external circuit, and this produces a potential difference.

concepts.term: Overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.def: The overall reaction involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Water is the only product of the reaction in the cell.

concepts.term: Fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries
concepts.def: Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries. A fuel cell needs no recharging time and keeps working while fuel is supplied, and the only product of the reaction is water; but hydrogen is difficult to store and to distribute safely, and rechargeable batteries can be refilled with energy from any electricity supply.
An equation for what happens at one electrode alone, showing the electrons that are lost or gained. In a half equation both the atoms and the total charge must balance on the two sides.

concepts.term: Negative electrode of the hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.def: Hydrogen is oxidised, losing electrons: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. The electrons released travel round the external circuit. (In a cell with an alkaline electrolyte the same oxidation is written 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻.)

concepts.term: Positive electrode of the hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.def: Oxygen is reduced, gaining the electrons that arrive from the circuit: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. (In a cell with an alkaline electrolyte the reduction is written O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.) Adding the two half equations gives the overall reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

mcqs.q: A chemical cell is connected to a bulb and the bulb lights. Where does the electricity come from?
options: From a reaction between the chemicals inside the cell
From electricity stored in the cell when it was made
From a supply of electrons held ready in the metal case
From the air, which reacts with the metal parts of it
mcqs.explain: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity; the reaction happens once the circuit is complete.

mcqs.q: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors. Which of these is one of them?
options: The size of the two pieces of metal used as electrodes
How long the cell was stored away before its first use
The type of metal used for each of the two electrodes
The length of the wire joining the cell to the circuit
mcqs.explain: The specification names the type of electrode as one of the factors the voltage depends on.

mcqs.q: A cell made from zinc and copper in copper sulfate solution gives 1.1 V. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by sodium chloride solution. What happens to the voltage?
options: It stays at 1.1 V, because the two metals are unchanged
It stays at 1.1 V, because the electrodes are the same size
It falls to zero, because sodium chloride is not an electrolyte
It changes, because voltage depends on the electrolyte used
mcqs.explain: The type of electrolyte is one of the named factors, so a different electrolyte can give a different voltage.

mcqs.q: What is needed to make a simple cell?
options: Two pieces of the same metal in contact with an electrolyte
Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte
Two different metals joined together by a length of wire
Two different metals dipped into a beaker of pure water
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the arrangement the specification gives for a simple cell.

mcqs.q: Which of these arrangements will produce a voltage?
options: Zinc and copper strips dipping into a beaker of pure water
Zinc and copper strips dipping into sodium chloride solution
Two copper strips dipping into copper sulfate solution
Zinc and copper strips held apart in air and joined by wire
mcqs.explain: Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, which is what a simple cell requires.

mcqs.q: What is a battery?
options: Another name for a single cell containing chemicals
Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater current
Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater voltage
A cell that can be recharged by an external electrical current
mcqs.explain: The specification's definition: cells joined in series so that their voltages add.

mcqs.q: Four identical 1.5 V cells are connected together in series to make a battery. What is the voltage of the battery?
mcqs.explain: Cells in series add: 4 x 1.5 V = 6.0 V, which is the greater voltage a battery provides.

mcqs.q: Why does a non-rechargeable cell eventually stop producing electricity?
options: The store of electrons inside it has all been given out
The electricity put in when it was made has been used up
One of the reactants inside it has been completely used up
The electrolyte has evaporated and can no longer conduct
mcqs.explain: The reactions stop when a reactant runs out, which is the specification's explanation.

mcqs.q: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?
options: They are rechargeable because they contain an alkali
They are non-rechargeable, so they cannot be recharged
They can be recharged by connecting a power supply
They recharge themselves slowly if they are left unused
mcqs.explain: The specification states plainly that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.

mcqs.q: Why can a rechargeable cell be recharged?
options: An external current pushes fresh chemicals into the cell
An external current refills the cell's store of electrons
An external current warms the cell so the reaction restarts
An external electrical current reverses the chemical reactions
mcqs.explain: This is the reason the specification gives for rechargeable cells being rechargeable.

mcqs.q: A rechargeable cell has gone flat and is connected to a charger. What happens inside the cell?
options: The products of the reaction are turned back into reactants
New reactants are supplied to the cell through the electrodes
Electrical charge is stored between the electrodes for later
The electrolyte is replaced by a fresh conducting solution
mcqs.explain: The current reverses the chemical reactions, re-forming the reactants that had been used up.

mcqs.q: Cells are made using a copper electrode and a second metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V, tin 0.5 V. What do these data show?
options: Metals close together in the reactivity series give the biggest voltage
The bigger the difference in reactivity, the bigger the voltage
The heavier the second metal is, the smaller the voltage produced
The more reactive the second metal, the smaller the voltage made
mcqs.explain: Magnesium is furthest from copper in reactivity and gives the largest voltage; tin is nearest and gives the smallest.

mcqs.q: A simple cell is made from magnesium and copper in an electrolyte. Which electrode is the negative one?
options: Copper, because the less reactive metal releases the electrons
Whichever metal is the larger piece dipped into the liquid
Magnesium, because it is the lighter of the two metals used
Magnesium, because it is the more reactive of the two metals
mcqs.explain: The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily, so it becomes the negative electrode.

mcqs.q: Which statement is a valid reason for choosing a rechargeable battery instead of an alkaline battery?
options: Alkaline batteries need recharging more often than it does
It can be recharged and reused, so less waste is produced
Recharging adds new chemicals, so it will never wear out
It produces a higher voltage than an alkaline battery does
mcqs.explain: The reactions are reversed by an external current, so one battery does the work of many.

mcqs.q: How is a hydrogen fuel cell kept working?
options: It is recharged from the mains when its fuel has run out
The hydrogen inside it is burned to heat the electrolyte
Hydrogen and oxygen or air are supplied to it from outside
Its used electrolyte is drained off and topped up with new
mcqs.explain: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the fuel in a fuel cell is correct?
options: It is oxidised electrochemically, producing a potential difference
It is burned in oxygen, and the heat produced makes electricity
It is stored inside the cell and is used up as the cell works
It is split by an electric current into hydrogen and oxygen
mcqs.explain: The oxidation happens at an electrode, so the electrons transferred pass through the circuit.

mcqs.q: What does the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell produce?
options: Water, from the oxidation of hydrogen
Carbon dioxide, from burning fuel
Hydrogen peroxide, from H₂ and O₂
Oxygen, released at the electrode
mcqs.explain: The overall reaction involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
options: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂
2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen is oxidised to water and the equation balances: four H and two O on each side.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a rechargeable battery?
options: It can be recharged far more quickly than a battery can be
It produces a much higher voltage than any battery can give
It stores much more electricity inside it than a battery does
It keeps working while fuel is supplied, with no recharging time
mcqs.explain: The fuel comes from an external source, so the cell is refuelled rather than left to recharge.

mcqs.q: Which is a disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries?
options: There are no disadvantages, so they will replace batteries
They release carbon dioxide from the cell as they work
Hydrogen is difficult to store and to distribute safely
The water they produce has to be stored inside the cell
mcqs.explain: A supply of hydrogen must be produced, stored under pressure and delivered, which batteries do not need.

mcqs.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?
options: H₂ → 2H⁺ + e⁻
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen is oxidised, losing electrons; atoms and charge both balance.

mcqs.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?
options: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O
O₂ + 4H⁺ → 2H₂O + 4e⁻
O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
mcqs.explain: Oxygen gains the electrons arriving from the circuit and is reduced to water; atoms and charge balance.
